claims.text: The initial system is a zirconium-alloy fuel-cladding substrate directly coated with elemental Cr.
A directly deposited elemental Cr coating on zirconium alloy is prone to elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion can cause premature coating failure.
A silicide interlayer should be deposited between the Zr-alloy substrate and the elemental Cr coating.
The silicide interlayer should have an optimized thickness on the order of tens of micrometers.
The silicide interlayer will minimize Cr and Zr interdiffusion at elevated temperatures.
Suppressing Cr–Zr interdiffusion will preserve coating integrity and prevent premature failure in accident-relevant steam.
The silicide layer participates in forming an oxide scale at high oxidation temperatures.
The oxide scale formed with participation of the silicide layer is protective.
The silicide-assisted protective oxide scale will operate under normal subcritical-water conditions.
Normal-operation conditions are represented by subcritical water below 350 °C, including a proposed test near 300 °C.
Accident-relevant conditions are represented by steam exposure at approximately 1000–1300 °C.
Relative to the directly Cr-coated baseline, the interlayer-modified system will exhibit significantly less Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Relative to the baseline, the interlayer-modified system will degrade more slowly during high-temperature steam exposure.
Relative to the baseline, the interlayer-modified system will maintain protective oxide performance during prolonged subcritical-water exposure.
The intervention can be implemented without adversely affecting metallurgical bonding or coating adhesion.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in Cr–Zr interdiffusion, or observation of worse oxidation protection or adhesion than the baseline, would falsify the hypothesis.
